title: Simulating Human Memory with Language Models
claim: Humans forget stimuli on memory tasks, while frontier models recall them near-perfectly, so models are unrealistic as human simulators.
layout: 3 columns by 3 rows, top-down; stimulus, human, LLM rows, color-coded
description: A 3x3 grid of rounded cards. Column headers read Reverse Digit Span, Narrative Free Recall and Map Task. The top row has gray cards with the task stimulus. These are the digits 281901451, the opening of a story about Emma and old maps, and a route Harbor → Warehouse → Quarry → Embassy. The middle row is pink and labeled Human, with a sad-face person icon. It shows a short wrong digit sequence (15409), a paraphrased story ("Emma always liked maps...") and three of five dots filled. The bottom row is green and labeled LLM, with a chip icon. It shows a near-complete digit recall, a verbatim story and five of five dots filled. Pink against green makes the human-versus-LLM gap clear. The eye goes first to the colored rows.
caption: Three sample tasks from our benchmark. In reverse digit span, participants must read and recall lists of numbers in reverse order; in narrative free recall, participants must read short stories and repeat them as precisely as possible; in the map task, participants must memorize a map and answer questions about routes between locations. Humans are limited in their ability to remember the stimuli and complete each of these tasks, whereas frontier LLMs perform at ceiling.
abstract: Language models are increasingly being deployed as user simulators, but their memory is far more reliable than that of real users. To measure this gap, we run a series of classic memory experiments from psychology on both humans and language models. Across tasks, we find that out-of-the-box language models exhibit better memory than humans, even when prompted to imitate human behavior. We then show that better prompting strategies and the use of a compactor can cause language models to forget content in a more human-like way. Using these methods, we show preliminary evidence that language models with human-like memory constraints can function as more effective user simulators in a downstream education task. Finally, we release human reference data and benchmarks to support future work on simulating human memory with language models.
